Sorted by $|\\Delta|$ descending.}\n\\end{table}\n\n\\section{Per-Task Dose-Response Breakdown}\n\\label{app:dose-response}\n\nTable~\\ref{tab:dose-response-detail} reports per-task death rates for Reflexion at $N{=}3$, 4, and 5 on the 10 death-prone tasks ($n{=}20$ episodes per task). Per-task variance is high (up to 25\\,pp range for \\texttt{measure-melting-point}), but the aggregate smooths to a 2.5\\,pp band, confirming that the plateau conclusion is robust at the aggregate level despite task-level noise. \\texttt{freeze} is consistently the hardest task (50--60\\% DR across all $N$).\n\n\\begin{table}[h]\n\\centering\n\\small\n\\caption{Per-task death rates (\\%) for Reflexion at $N{=}3$, 4, 5 on 10 death-prone tasks ($n{=}20$ per task). Aggregate death rates confirm the plateau at $N \\geq 3$ (range: $34.0$--$36.5\\%$).}\n\\label{tab:dose-response-detail}\n\\begin{tabular}{@{}lrrr@{}}\n\\toprule\nTask & $N{=}3$ & $N{=}4$ & $N{=}5$ \\\\\n\\midrule\nchemistry-mix & 25.0 & 35.0 & 20.0 \\\\\nfind-animal & 45.0 & 30.0 & 45.0 \\\\\nfreeze & 50.0 & 50.0 & 60.0 \\\\\ngrow-fruit & 30.0 & 25.0 & 25.0 \\\\\nidentify-life-stages-1 & 35.0 & 35.0 & 35.0 \\\\\nidentify-life-stages-2 & 25.0 & 25.0 & 30.0 \\\\\ninclined-plane-angle & 20.0 & 30.0 & 35.0 \\\\\nlifespan-longest & 45.0 & 40.0 & 40.0 \\\\\nlifespan-long+short & 30.0 & 45.0 & 35.0 \\\\\nmeasure-melting-pt & 35.0 & 50.0 & 25.0 \\\\\n\\midrule\n\\textbf{Aggregate} & \\textbf{34.0} & \\textbf{36.5} & \\textbf{35.0} \\\\\n\\bottomrule\n\\end{tabular}\n\\end{table}\n\n\\section{Router Training Details}\n\\label{app:router-details}\n\nWe use Qwen3-1.7B for the router to avoid circular dependency with the Qwen2.5-7B data-generating model.\n\nWith gradient accumulation of 1 (effective batch size 4), routing performance is highly sensitive to the evaluation split; this suggests overfitting to specific train/validation partition boundaries. With gradient accumulation of 8 (effective batch size 32), step-level performance stabilizes across splits (${\\sim}54\\%$ balanced accuracy). All reported results use gradient accumulation 8.\n\nUnder step-level evaluation with a fixed data split, cross-seed balanced accuracy ranges from 52.7\\% to 58.1\\%, but internal recall varies from 51.5\\% to 81.8\\%, which reflects threshold sensitivity. However, episode-level evaluation reveals that this apparent discrimination does not generalize: balanced accuracy drops to $47.1 \\pm 2.2\\%$ across 8 cross-split seeds (Appendix~\\ref{app:seed-robustness}). Deployed end-to-end, the trained router allocates 97.0\\% of episodes to deterministic computation with 17.6\\% death rate, and misrouting cost (death from internally-routed episodes) exceeds the benefit of correctly routing rare internal-preferred cases.\n\n\\paragraph{Evaluation methods.} All results use \\emph{generation-based evaluation}: the model generates a routing label as text (\\texttt{enable\\_thinking=False}), parsed for classification. We evaluate at two granularities: \\emph{step-level} (steps from the same episode may appear in both train and validation sets) and \\emph{episode-level} (entire episodes held out). Step-level accuracy ($54.1 \\pm 5.4\\%$) exceeds chance (the router captures some signal), but episode-level accuracy ($47.1 \\pm 2.2\\%$, below chance) shows this does not generalize to unseen episodes. Augmentation-based data scaling (Appendix~\\ref{app:seed-robustness}) provides no improvement; real-data scaling remains open. Always-deterministic is trivially near-optimal given DAF $= 90.4\\%$. The main text (\\S\\ref{sec:router-diagnostic}) reports controlled 4-seed results at three scales; the model-size ablation (Appendix~\\ref{app:ablations}) provides further detail.\n\n\\begin{table}[h]\n\\centering\n\\small\n\\resizebox{\\columnwidth}{!}{%\n\\begin{tabular}{@{}lcc@{}}\n\\toprule\nHyperparameter & Classification Head & Implicit Router \\\\\n\\midrule\nBase model & Qwen3-1.7B & Qwen3-1.7B \\\\\nArchitecture & Linear + LoRA & SFT + LoRA \\\\\nLoRA $r$ / $\\alpha$ & 16 / 32 & 16 / 32 \\\\\nLearning rate & 2e-5 & 2e-4 \\\\\nOptimizer & AdamW & AdamW \\\\\nEpochs & 3 & 3 \\\\\nBatch size (per device) & 4 & 4 \\\\\nGradient accumulation & 8 & 8 \\\\\nWarmup ratio & 0.1 & 0.1 \\\\\nWeight decay & 0.01 & 0.01 \\\\\nMax sequence length & 512 & 512 \\\\\nSeeds & \\{42\\} & \\{42, 123, 456, 789\\} \\\\\n\\bottomrule\n\\end{tabular}}\n\\caption{Router training hyperparameters. Both architectures use the same base model with LoRA adaptation. The classification head degenerates across all configurations; the implicit router results are reported as 4-seed mean$\\pm$std.}\n\\label{tab:hyperparams}\n\\end{table}\n\n\\section{Seed Robustness}\n\\label{app:seed-robustness}\n\nWe assess router generalization at two evaluation granularities: \\emph{step-level}, where steps from the same episode may appear in both train and validation sets, and \\emph{episode-level}, where entire episodes are held out. Both use cross-split evaluation (seeds $\\{42, \\ldots, 49\\}$, 8 seeds total), where the data partition and training seed both vary. Table~\\ref{tab:seed-robustness} reports per-seed results.\n\n\\begin{table}[h]\n\\centering\n\\small\n\\begin{tabular}{@{}llcc@{}}\n\\toprule\nEval.\\ Granularity & Seed & Bal.\\ Acc.\\ (\\%) \\\\\n\\midrule\nStep-level & 42 & 57.06 \\\\\n(same-episode & 43 & 63.99 \\\\\nleakage) & 44 & 55.43 \\\\\n & 45 & 56.14 \\\\\n & 46 & 55.45 \\\\\n & 47 & 50.08 \\\\\n & 48 & 48.03 \\\\\n & 49 & 59.30 \\\\\n\\cmidrule{2-3}\n & Mean$\\pm$std & $54.1 \\pm 5.4$ \\\\\n\\midrule\nEpisode-level & 42 & 48.1 \\\\\n(held-out & 43 & 47.9 \\\\\nepisodes) & 44 & 49.6 \\\\\n & 45 & 49.4 \\\\\n & 46 & 48.5 \\\\\n & 47 & 43.1 \\\\\n & 48 & 45.4 \\\\\n & 49 & 44.8 \\\\\n\\cmidrule{2-3}\n & Mean$\\pm$std & $47.1 \\pm 2.2$ \\\\\n\\midrule\n\\multicolumn{2}{@{}l}{Always-det (= majority-vote)} & 50.0 \\\\\n\\bottomrule\n\\end{tabular}\n\\caption{Per-seed router performance under cross-split evaluation (8 seeds, generation-based, \\texttt{enable\\_thinking=False}). Step-level evaluation allows steps from the same episode in both train and validation sets (same-episode leakage). Episode-level evaluation holds out entire episodes; the resulting $47.1 \\pm 2.2\\%$ is below the 50\\% chance baseline. A data scaling ablation (Table~\\ref{tab:data-scaling}) confirms this is structural rather than data-limited.}\n\\label{tab:seed-robustness}\n\\end{table}\n\nThe contrast between step-level ($54.1 \\pm 5.4\\%$) and episode-level ($47.1 \\pm 2.2\\%$) evaluation reveals a generalization gap: the step-level signal likely reflects memorization of episode-specific context (enabled by same-episode leakage) rather than extraction of generalizable routing features. At episode level, the router performs below chance across all 8 seeds (range: 43.1\\%--49.6\\%). Augmentation-based data scaling (Table~\\ref{tab:data-scaling}) from 25\\% to 800\\% ($32{\\times}$ range) provides no improvement, converging to the always-deterministic baseline ($50\\%$). However, paraphrase augmentation inflates the majority class without generating novel routing patterns; real-data scaling remains an open question. With DAF $= 90.4\\%$ and all task types deterministic-majority (86:9 label ratio), always-deterministic trivially solves the episode-level routing problem, leaving no learnable signal for a step-level router.\n\n\\paragraph{Data scaling ablation.} To test whether the episode-level generalization failure stems from data scarcity, we vary training set size from 25\\% to 800\\% of the original via paraphrase-based data augmentation (synonym substitution + template variation on step observations), holding the episode-level validation set fixed. Table~\\ref{tab:data-scaling} reports the results.\n\n\\begin{table}[h]\n\\centering\n\\small\n\\begin{tabular}{@{}rccc@{}}\n\\toprule\nScale & Samples & Det\\% & Ep.\\ Bal.\\ Acc.\\ (\\%) \\\\\n\\midrule\n25\\% & 433 & ${\\sim}90$ & $49.5 \\pm 0.3$ \\\\\n50\\% & 867 & ${\\sim}90$ & $51.5$ \\\\\n100\\% & 1{,}735 & 89.6 & $49.9 \\pm 0.1$ \\\\\n200\\% & 3{,}470 & 94.2 & $50.0 \\pm 0.0$ \\\\\n800\\% & 13{,}880 & ${\\sim}97.7$ & $51.0 \\pm 1.1$ \\\\\n\\midrule\nAlways-det & --- & --- & 50.0 \\\\\n\\bottomrule\n\\end{tabular}\n\\caption{Data scaling ablation: episode-level balanced accuracy across training set sizes (25\\%--800\\% of original, $32{\\times}$ range). Internal recall $= 0.0$ at all scales (complete majority-class collapse). Det\\%: fraction of deterministic-preferred labels in training data. The 50\\% scale is a single seed; all others report mean$\\pm$std across seeds.}\n\\label{tab:data-scaling}\n\\end{table}\n\nAll scales hover at ${\\sim}50\\%$ episode-level balanced accuracy (equivalent to the always-deterministic baseline), with no monotonic improvement as data increases. Augmentation-based scaling provides no improvement at any scale; however, episode-level minority-class diversity remains a potential confound that cannot be resolved without collecting more internal-preferred episodes. The ground-truth internal-preferred rate (9/245 $= 3.7\\%$) means collecting 50 internal-preferred episodes would require approximately 1{,}350 paired episodes at current environment dynamics, a $5.5{\\times}$ expansion with diminishing return on a $9.6\\%$ signal. The failure points instead to a structural limitation: when DAF $= 90.4\\%$ and all task types are deterministic-majority (86:9 label ratio), the episode-level routing problem is trivially solved by always choosing deterministic, leaving no learnable signal for a step-level router to exploit.\n\nAugmentation disproportionately increases the majority (deterministic) class: Det\\% rises from 89.6\\% at 100\\% to 94.2\\% at 200\\% and ${\\sim}97.7\\%$ at 800\\%. However, the complete collapse to majority-class prediction (internal recall $= 0.0$) occurs even at the smallest unaugmented scale (25\\%, ${\\sim}90\\%$ det); this is not an augmentation artifact. Balanced accuracy corrects for class imbalance by averaging per-class recall, so the metric itself is not biased by the skew.\n\nDecomposition metrics are stable under bootstrap resampling (1{,}000 resamples of the 245-episode dataset): DAF $= 90.6\\% \\pm 4.2\\%$ (95\\% CI $[81.6\\%, 98.8\\%]$); Pearson $r = 0.975 \\pm 0.011$ (95\\% CI $[0.952, 0.995]$). The death avoidance dominance finding is robust to both resampling and split perturbation.\n\n\\paragraph{Per-task-type evaluation breakdown.} To test whether the router learns transferable routing strategies or merely task-type classification, we evaluate existing checkpoints (8 seeds) separately on each of the 11 task types. Of the 11 task types, 7 have \\emph{all-deterministic} labels (no internal-preferred episodes exist), making balanced accuracy undefined; the router has nothing to learn beyond the trivial always-deterministic default. For the remaining 4 task types where both classes are present, balanced accuracy ranges from 50.0\\% to 73.0\\%, but this apparent signal does not indicate cross-task-type routing transfer: the router is effectively classifying task types (which correlate with death risk) rather than extracting a generalizable routing strategy. This complements the data scaling ablation: routing signal does not transfer across task types because the signal \\emph{is} the task type, i.e., whether a given task carries death risk. The 4B capacity scaling result (Appendix~\\ref{app:ablations}) suggests capacity is one factor, but even 4B's $59.0\\%$ episode-level accuracy does not demonstrate cross-task-type transfer.\n\n\\section{Penalty Sensitivity Analysis}\n\\label{app:penalty}\n\n\\begin{table}[h]\n\\centering\n\\small\n\\begin{tabular}{@{}rrr@{}}\n\\toprule\n$P$ & DAF($P$) & 95\\% CI \\\\\n\\midrule\n0 & 7.5\\% & [$-36.7$, $83.1$] \\\\\n10 & 50.4\\% & [$19.8$, $94.5$] \\\\\n25 & 70.8\\% & [$48.5$, $97.1$] \\\\\n50 & 82.6\\% & [$67.6$, $98.4$] \\\\\n100\\textsuperscript{*} & 90.4\\% & [$81.5$, $99.1$] \\\\\n200 & 95.0\\% & [$90.0$, $99.5$] \\\\\n500 & 97.9\\% & [$95.8$, $99.8$] \\\\\n\\bottomrule\n\\end{tabular}\n\\caption{Sensitivity of DAF to death penalty magnitude $P$. DAF$(P) = 1 - \\Delta_{\\text{nd}} / \\Delta_{\\text{full}}(P)$, where $\\Delta_{\\text{full}}(P) \\approx \\delta \\cdot P + \\Delta_{\\text{nd}}$, $\\delta = 0.2653$ is the death-rate differential, and $\\Delta_{\\text{nd}} = 2.84$ (strict neither-died filtering). Bootstrap 95\\% CIs from 1{,}000 resamples. \\textsuperscript{*}Default setting.}\n\\label{tab:penalty-sensitivity}\n\\end{table}\n\nThe non-death score gap $\\Delta_{\\text{nd}} = 2.84$ is invariant across penalty levels; it depends only on surviving-episode performance, not on $P$. As $P$ increases, $\\Delta_{\\text{full}}$ grows ($16.33$ at $P{=}50$, $29.60$ at $P{=}100$, $56.13$ at $P{=}200$) while $\\Delta_{\\text{nd}}$ remains fixed, mechanically increasing DAF.\n\n\\paragraph{Mechanism boundary: death specificity.}\nThe $r = 0.97$ correlation between per-task death-rate differential and $\\Delta_{\\text{full}}$ is specific to catastrophic death (score $= -100$). Broader failure definitions dissolve the correlation entirely: defining ``failure'' as any non-positive score ($T{=}0$) yields $r = -0.13$ ($p = 0.70$), because non-death episodes show near-zero performance differential between strategies ($\\Delta_{\\text{nd}} = 2.84$). Table~\\ref{tab:penalty-correlation} quantifies this specificity across penalty magnitudes.\n\n\\begin{table}[h]\n\\centering\n\\small\n\\begin{tabular}{@{}rccl@{}}\n\\toprule\n$P$ & $r$ & $p$ & Sig.\\ ($\\alpha{=}0.05$) \\\\\n\\midrule\n10 & $-0.08$ & $0.813$ & No \\\\\n25 & $0.51$ & $0.108$ & No \\\\\n50 & $0.86$ & $0.0006$ & Yes \\\\\n100\\textsuperscript{*} & $0.97$ & $8 \\times 10^{-7}$ & Yes \\\\\n200 & $0.99$ & $1 \\times 10^{-9}$ & Yes \\\\\n\\bottomrule\n\\end{tabular}\n\\caption{Pearson $r$ between per-task death-rate differential and $\\Delta_{\\text{full}}(P)$ across penalty magnitudes. The correlation is non-significant at low penalties and emerges at $P \\geq 50$, which reflects the transition from non-death-dominated to death-dominated score gaps. \\textsuperscript{*}Default ScienceWorld setting.}\n\\label{tab:penalty-correlation}\n\\end{table}\n\nThis sharpens our central finding: death is not merely the dominant component of routing signal; it is effectively the \\emph{only} component that generates differential routing signal in ScienceWorld. At low penalties, the death contribution is small and $\\Delta_{\\text{full}}$ reduces to $\\Delta_{\\text{nd}} \\approx 2.84$, which is near-uniform across task types ($\\text{mean non-death gap} = -1.19$ excluding the \\texttt{find-non-living-thing} outlier); consequently, death-rate differential has no predictive power. As $P$ increases, the death term dominates $\\Delta_{\\text{full}}$, and the correlation sharpens because death rates \\emph{are} the performance gap. The DAF values in Table~\\ref{tab:penalty-sensitivity} increase monotonically with $P$, but this is a mathematical consequence of the decomposition ($\\text{DAF} = \\delta P / (\\delta P + \\Delta_{\\text{nd}})$), not evidence of mechanism robustness.\n\n\\section{Cross-Environment Details}\n\\label{app:cross-env-details}\n\n\\begin{figure}[h]\n\\centering\n\\includegraphics[width=\\columnwidth]{figures/signal_reversal.pdf}\n\\caption{Cross-environment label distributions. ScienceWorld and ALFWorld both show deterministic preference, but through different mechanisms: death avoidance (ScienceWorld) vs.\\ information asymmetry from admissible-action access (ALFWorld). MATH shows balanced labels, confirming no routing signal without catastrophic failure.}\n\\label{fig:signal-reversal}\n\\end{figure}\n\n\\begin{table}[h]\n\\centering\n\\small\n\\resizebox{\\columnwidth}{!}{%\n\\begin{tabular}{@{}lccccc@{}}\n\\toprule\nEnvironment & $N$ & Det\\% & Int\\% & NoPref\\% & Death? \\\\\n\\midrule\nScienceWorld & 245 & 35.1 & 3.7 & 61.2 & Yes ($-100$) \\\\\nMATH & 795 & 12.0 & 13.5 & 74.6 & No \\\\\nALFWorld & 135 & 25.9 & 1.5 & 72.6 & No\\textsuperscript{$\\dagger$} \\\\\n\\bottomrule\n\\end{tabular}}\n\\caption{Cross-environment label distribution. ``Deterministic'' denotes qualitatively different modalities per environment. $\\dagger$\\,ALFWorld's deterministic advantage stems from information asymmetry, not death avoidance.}\n\\label{tab:cross-env}\n\\end{table}\n\n\\section{Cross-Model Verification}\n\\label{app:cross-model}\n\nWe replicate the counterfactual analysis with Llama-3.1-8B-Instruct across all 11 task types ($N{=}220$ episode pairs, 20 per type; Table~\\ref{tab:cross-model-detail}).\nThe internal strategy dies in $41.4\\%$ of episodes versus $11.4\\%$ for deterministic (death-rate differential $+30.0$~pp), with 83 deterministic-preferred, 3 internal-preferred (1.4\\%, all death-asymmetry reversals), and 134 no-preference labels.\nBoth models exhibit nearly identical internal vulnerability (${\\sim}$42\\%: Qwen $42.9\\%$, Llama $41.4\\%$), confirming that death-prone failure is structurally determined. The differential magnitude varies ($+26.5$~pp Qwen, $+30.0$~pp Llama) because deterministic strategy safety is model-dependent ($16.3\\%$ vs.\\ $11.4\\%$), but directional consistency is 100\\% (10/10 death-prone tasks in both models).\n\\texttt{identify-life-stages-1} shows cross-model precision matching ($55\\%$/$10\\%$/$+45$~pp in both models).\n\\texttt{find-non-living-thing} shows zero deaths in both models, consistent with its majority-class answer distribution.\n\n\\begin{table}[h]\n\\centering\n\\small\n\\begin{tabular}{@{}lrrrl@{}}\n\\toprule\nTask & Int\\% & Det\\% & $\\Delta$\\,pp & D / I / N \\\\\n\\midrule\nidentify-life-stages-1 & 55 & 10 & +45 & 9 / 0 / 11 \\\\\nfreeze & 45 & 0 & +45 & 9 / 0 / 11 \\\\\ngrow-fruit & 45 & 5 & +40 & 8 / 0 / 12 \\\\\nidentify-life-stages-2 & 45 & 5 & +40 & 8 / 0 / 12 \\\\\nmeasure-melting-point & 50 & 15 & +35 & 9 / 0 / 11 \\\\\nlifespan-longest & 35 & 5 & +30 & 7 / 1 / 12 \\\\\nlifespan-l-then-s & 50 & 20 & +30 & 6 / 0 / 14 \\\\\nchemistry-mix & 45 & 20 & +25 & 5 / 0 / 15 \\\\\ninclined-plane & 45 & 20 & +25 & 6 / 0 / 14 \\\\\nfind-animal & 40 & 25 & +15 & 6 / 2 / 12 \\\\\nfind-non-living-thing & 0 & 0 & 0 & 10 / 0 / 10 \\\\\n\\midrule\n\\textbf{Aggregate} & \\textbf{41.4} & \\textbf{11.4} & \\textbf{+30.0} & \\textbf{83 / 3 / 134} \\\\\n\\bottomrule\n\\end{tabular}\n\\caption{Per-task Llama-3.1-8B cross-model replication ($N{=}20$ per task). D/I/N: deterministic-preferred / internal-preferred / no-preference. Sorted by $\\Delta$ DR descending.}\n\\label{tab:cross-model-detail}\n\\end{table}\n\n\\section{Failure Mode Analysis}\n\\label{app:failure-modes}\n\nAll 105 internal-strategy deaths (100\\%) are triggered by the same action pattern: \\texttt{focus on [object]}. In ScienceWorld, \\texttt{focus on} is the answer-submission action (equivalent to ``this is my final answer''); the LLM agent systematically misuses it as a general interaction or exploration command, and applies it to irrelevant targets (rooms, doors, inventory items). Each such execution submits an incorrect answer and triggers the $-100$ death penalty. Within death episodes, both strategies exhibit comparable \\texttt{focus on} rates (${\\sim}5\\%$); the internal strategy's higher death count (105 vs.\\ 40 for deterministic) reflects how often each strategy enters catastrophic states, not different action selection within those states.\n\nManual inspection identifies four failure categories: (A) no task awareness, where the agent executes \\texttt{focus on} without reading the task; (B) task-aware but lacking action grounding, where the agent correctly identifies the objective but cannot map it to valid action primitives; (D) genuine attempts with execution failure; and (E) initial progress wasted by early errors. Category B dominates: agents demonstrate task comprehension but systematically fail to translate it into correct ScienceWorld actions.\n\\label{tab:death-taxonomy}\n\n\\paragraph{Representative examples.}\n\\emph{Category A} (no task awareness): In a \\texttt{chemistry-mix} episode, the agent immediately executes \\texttt{focus on kitchen}, \\texttt{focus on door}, \\texttt{focus on inventory} without reading the task, dying on the first \\texttt{focus on} call. \\emph{Category B} (comprehension without grounding): In a \\texttt{lifespan-longest-lived} episode, the agent correctly identifies that it must compare animal lifespans and reasons about which animal lives longest, but then executes \\texttt{focus on oak tree} (a non-animal object in the room) instead of navigating to find the target animal, triggering death.\n\n\\paragraph{Action distribution analysis.}\nFigure~\\ref{fig:death-action-dist} shows the action distribution in death versus non-death episodes for the internal strategy; both are dominated by \\texttt{connect} actions, with \\texttt{focus on} moderately more frequent in death episodes ($5.4\\%$ vs.\\ $3.4\\%$). Crucially, Figure~\\ref{fig:death-comparison} reveals that within death episodes, internal and deterministic strategies exhibit comparable \\texttt{focus on} rates (${\\sim}5\\%$). The survival gap (105 vs.\\ 40 deaths) therefore reflects how often each strategy enters catastrophic states, not how it behaves within those states. Among fatal \\texttt{focus on} targets, \\texttt{workshop} remains the most frequent (20.0\\%), followed by \\texttt{inventory} (17.1\\%) and \\texttt{kitchen} (10.5\\%), indicating a systematic object bias rather than random exploration. Figure~\\ref{fig:death-timeline} visualizes the temporal pattern: agents execute long sequences of \\texttt{connect} actions before a terminal \\texttt{focus on} triggers death, typically in the final 1--3 steps.\n\n\\begin{figure}[h]\n\\centering\n\\includegraphics[width=\\columnwidth]{figures/death_action_distribution.pdf}\n\\caption{Action distribution for the internal (LLM) strategy in death ($n{=}105$) vs.\\ non-death ($n{=}140$) episodes. Left: full distribution (both dominated by \\texttt{connect}). Right: non-\\texttt{connect} actions zoomed. \\texttt{focus on} is moderately more frequent in death episodes ($5.4\\%$ vs.\\ $3.4\\%$), while non-death episodes show higher rates of observation and object interaction.}\n\\label{fig:death-action-dist}\n\\end{figure}\n\n\\begin{figure}[h]\n\\centering\n\\includegraphics[width=\\columnwidth]{figures/death_action_timeline.pdf}\n\\caption{Step-by-step action sequences for 6 representative death episodes. The fatal \\texttt{focus on} action (marked with arrow) consistently appears in the final steps after long \\texttt{connect} sequences, and illustrates the ``connect loop $\\to$ fatal focus'' pattern. Examples are drawn from the full 30-task dataset for task-type diversity; the pattern is identical in the 11-task analysis subset.}\n\\label{fig:death-timeline}\n\\end{figure}\n\n\\begin{figure}[h]\n\\centering\n\\includegraphics[width=\\columnwidth]{figures/death_action_comparison.pdf}\n\\caption{Non-\\texttt{connect} action distribution comparison between internal (left) and deterministic (right) strategies. Within death episodes, both strategies exhibit comparable \\texttt{focus on} rates (${\\sim}5\\%$); the internal strategy's higher death count (105 vs.\\ 40) reflects more frequent entry into catastrophic states, not different action selection within those states.}\n\\label{fig:death-comparison}\n\\end{figure}\n\n\\section{Grounding Ablation}\n\\label{app:grounding-ablation}\n\nWe test whether directly intervening on the dominant death action (\\texttt{focus on}) eliminates death vulnerability on the 10 death-prone tasks (baseline 48.0\\%, $n{=}200$).\n\n\\paragraph{Prompt warning.} Adding an explicit system prompt (``use \\texttt{focus on} only for final answers'') reduces aggregate death rate to 37.0\\% ($\\Delta = -11$~pp). Both identification tasks exhibit ironic effects (\\texttt{identify-life-stages-1}: 35\\%$\\to$50\\%; \\texttt{identify-life-stages-2}: 25\\%$\\to$70\\%), where explicit mention of the dangerous action may have increased its salience.\n\n\\paragraph{Action-space filtering.} Blocking \\texttt{focus on} during the exploration phase yields 379 blocks across 200 episodes with zero leaks and zero passthroughs (the agent never persisted in retrying blocked actions), reducing death rate to 29.0\\% ($\\Delta = -19$~pp). The zero-passthrough rate suggests \\texttt{focus on} use is a shallow behavioral pattern rather than a deliberate strategy.\n\n\\paragraph{Per-task variation.} Under filtering, \\texttt{identify-life-stages} and \\texttt{inclined-plane} approach deterministic-level safety (${\\sim}$15--20\\% DR), while \\texttt{chemistry-mix} and \\texttt{find-animal} remain at 35--40\\%. Residual deaths occur during the answer-submission window, where the filter is inactive and agents submit \\texttt{focus on} to incorrect objects.\n\n\\section{Ablation Studies}\n\\label{app:ablations}\n\n\\paragraph{Capacity scaling.} We scale the implicit router from Qwen3-0.6B to Qwen3-4B and evaluate at both step and episode level (Table~\\ref{tab:capacity}).\n\n\\begin{table}[h]\n\\centering\n\\small\n\\begin{tabular}{@{}lcc@{}}\n\\toprule\nModel & Step Bal.\\ Acc.\\ (\\%) & Ep.\\ Bal.\\ Acc.\\ (\\%) \\\\\n\\midrule\nQwen3-0.6B & $56.4 \\pm 3.5$ & $50.7 \\pm 2.6$ \\\\\nQwen3-1.7B & $58.2 \\pm 4.0$ & $43.1 \\pm 1.0$ \\\\\nQwen3-4B & $59.2 \\pm 3.5$ & $\\mathbf{59.0 \\pm 1.9}$ \\\\\n\\midrule\nAlways-det & 50.0 & 50.0 \\\\\n\\bottomrule\n\\end{tabular}\n\\caption{Capacity scaling: step-level and episode-level balanced accuracy (4 seeds, identical configuration across all scales). Step-level accuracy is flat ($56$--$59\\%$, within seed variance). At episode level, only 4B breaks the random baseline ($59.0\\%$, $p < 0.005$).}\n\\label{tab:capacity}\n\\end{table}\n\nStep-level balanced accuracy is flat across scales ($56$--$59\\%$, within seed variance); step-level discrimination is not capacity-sensitive. At episode level, only 4B breaks the random baseline ($59.0 \\pm 1.9\\%$, $p < 0.005$); 0.6B and 1.7B remain at or below chance. The dominant explanation is that death avoidance constitutes a task-type-level binary signal that a step-level router cannot exploit efficiently.\n\n\\paragraph{Generative router.} A generative routing model trained with explicit routing labels achieves balanced accuracy of 46.7\\%, confirming that the routing bottleneck is signal-limited, not architecture-limited.\n\n\\paragraph{Leave-one-task-type-out routing.} Under leave-one-task-type-out evaluation, blind routing collapses to always-deterministic (balanced accuracy 50.0\\%); a keyword-based variant achieves 62.9\\% only through task-identity leakage, not genuine routing signal.\n\n\\paragraph{Reasoning depth.} An ablation comparing chain-of-thought reasoning against direct-answer generation on 6 task types ($n{=}120$ episodes per condition, 6 tasks $\\times$ 20 episodes per task) found no significant difference (Mann--Whitney $p > 0.26$, $|d| \\leq 0.31$) and near-identical death rates (41.8\\% vs.\\ 42.5\\%); reasoning depth does not meaningfully alter internal-mode outcomes.\n\n\\section{Threshold Routing Analysis}\n\\label{sec:threshold-routing}\n\nGiven per-task death risk knowledge, we test whether a simple threshold routing strategy can outperform always-deterministic. For each threshold $t \\in [0, 1]$, we route to internal if the per-task internal death rate $\\leq t$, otherwise to deterministic, and sweep all thresholds to find the optimal.\n\n\\begin{table}[h]\n\\centering\n\\small\n\\begin{tabular}{lccc}\n\\toprule\nStrategy & Mean Score & Death Rate & $\\Delta$ vs Det \\\\\n\\midrule\nAlways-det & $-9.47$ & $0.163$ & $0.00$ \\\\\nOptimal threshold ($t{=}0$) & $-11.03$ & $0.155$ & $-1.56$ \\\\\nAlways-internal & $-39.07$ & $0.429$ & $-29.60$ \\\\\n\\bottomrule\n\\end{tabular}\n\\caption{Death-risk threshold routing analysis on 245 episodes. The optimal threshold routes only \\texttt{find-non-living-thing} (the sole zero-death task) to internal, with all other tasks routed to deterministic. The LOTO-DAF analysis (Table in Appendix E, lines 229-259) shows:

So R1's point is that the 78.9% is driven by having 10 death-prone + 1 death-free task. If you had more death-free tasks, the percentage would drop.


The paper counters this with evidence that the signal is actually distributed across tasks (low SCI of 0.2147), the excluded tasks are even more death-prone than included ones, and sensitivity analysis shows individual task removal only shifts the metric by a few percentage points. R1 raises a valid structural concern about composition dependency, but the broader evidence suggests adding more tasks wouldn't substantially lower the metric since most excluded tasks are also death-dominated—though I see merit in both the paper's nuanced per-task breakdown and R1's point about the binary classification being potentially oversimplified.

Now looking at R1's second critique: they're pointing out that when the death penalty is removed entirely (P=0), 54 of the 75 death-asymmetry labels collapse into ties since both strategies score zero without the penalty. This means only 21 death-asymmetry labels remain meaningful at P=0, bringing the total non-tie count down to just 41, where death asymmetry represents 51.2% of the signal. The paper actually documents this exact finding in its own results section, so the data supports R1's calculation—the "penalty-independent" framing does obscure how heavily the metric depends on the death penalty's presence.

For the cluster inference concern, the paper cites the relevant methodological literature and provides supplementary validation through wild cluster bootstrap testing, which shows strong significance even under that more conservative approach.

The effect size is substantial at Cohen's d = 3.02, and the directional consistency across all tests is perfect, which gives me confidence in the robustness of the finding despite the small cluster count. I'd characterize this as something that warrants cautious interpretation of the confidence intervals rather than a fundamental problem with the conclusion.

On the pure-strategy decomposition, I see R1's point about practical implications for mixed strategies, but the paper's approach of using pure strategies as a diagnostic tool is methodologically sound for isolating what drives routing decisions—that's a different analytical question than what a mixed-strategy analysis would address.

For the figure caption issue, R1 is correct that the mathematical consequence caveat appears in the main text but not in the figure itself. Now for the 72B DAF calculation—there's a real asymmetry here. The paper computes DAF using 72B for the internal strategy but keeps the deterministic baseline fixed at 16.3% from the 7B model. That means we're comparing 72B internal performance against a 7B deterministic baseline, which isn't apples-to-apples. The concern is whether the deterministic strategy should also scale to 72B for a fair comparison.

On the mislabeling issue, the 27.7% step-level disagreement doesn't directly impact the 78.9% episode-level metric since they operate at different granularities. The paper does acknowledge in Appendix F that paraphrase augmentation inflates the majority class without creating novel routing patterns, though the main text conclusion reads stronger than that caveat suggests. I'm partially aligned with R1 here.

Looking at R1's specific questions: the paper doesn't explicitly state whether the 72B deterministic baseline uses a 7B or 72B model, which is a real gap. On the find-non-living-thing task with n=40, the footnote reveals they doubled the sample size after seeing it was a zero-death outlier—that's a data-dependent decision that R1 flagged correctly.

已完成全文和附录的复查。下面逐条回应 Reviewer 1 的意见。

---

## 逐条回应 Reviewer 1

### Must-Fix

**[AGREE] R1-N1**: 78.9% label fraction 是 task composition 的产物
- 同意核心论点。LOTO-DAF 表（Appendix E, Table 7）明确显示：移除唯一 death-free 任务 `find-non-living-thing` 后 DAF 跳至 100%，因为剩余 10 个 task types 的所有 non-tie labels 都来自 death asymmetry。78.9% 确实由 10:1 的 death-prone/death-free task 比例决定。
- **但有一个 nuance**：R1 建议将 framework 输出视为 binary classification ("此环境是否 death-dominated")。我认为这过于简化。SCI = 0.2147（§3.1）说明 death signal 在 task types 间分布较均匀，不是靠少数 outlier 驱动。Anti-cherry-picking 分析（Appendix C, Table 4）显示 18/19 excluded tasks 同样是 death-dominated（Δ DR = +38.2pp > +28.7pp）。所以即使增加更多 task types，78.9% 大概率不会大幅下降。但 R1 的结构性批评仍然成立——aggregate percentage 的信息量不如 per-task binary pattern。
- **建议**：作者应同时报告 binary diagnostic（"X/Y task types are death-dominated"）和连续 metric，而非仅以 78.9% 作为 headline。

**[AGREE] R1-N2**: "penalty-independent" 表述误导
- 强烈同意。论文自己的数据（§3.1, experiments.tex）明确说 "Of these 75, 54 (72.0%) reduce to ties when the death penalty is removed entirely"。这意味着在 P=0 时，effective non-tie count = 95 - 54 = 41，其中 death-asymmetry labels = 75 - 54 = 21，death-asymmetry fraction = 21/41 = 51.2%。这远低于论文宣称的 78.9%。
- R1 的计算完全正确。78.9% 看似 "penalty-independent" 是因为 labeling function（Algorithm 1, Appendix B, line 77-80）优先以 death status 分配标签——即使在 surviving strategy 也得 0 分的情况下，只要存在 death asymmetry 就分配非 tie 标签。这是 **labeling 设计的产物**，不是真正的 penalty-independence。
- 这与我的 N1（DAF 新颖性存疑）完全一致且互相加强。

**[REBUT] R1-N3**: K=11 cluster 推断可靠性不足
- 部分反驳。R1 引用 Cameron & Gelbach (2008) 和 Webb (2023) 关于 K<40 over-rejection 的结论在一般情况下成立，但此处的 effect size 异常大。Table 6（Appendix D）报告 Cohen's d = 3.02，directional consistency 10/10 on death-prone tasks（仅 `find-non-living-thing` 例外，且它是 zero-death by design）。
- 论文提供了四种独立检验（Appendix D）：cluster-robust t-test (p<0.001)、wild cluster bootstrap (p<0.001)、exact permutation test (p=0.002, 4/2048)、sign test (p<0.001)。Exact permutation 不依赖 asymptotic assumptions，在 K=11 下 p=0.002 仍然有效。
- **CI 宽度 [73%, 100%] 确实值得 caveat**，但这已经在 Limitations 中明确讨论（main.tex line 42: "cluster bootstrap with K=11 task-type clusters yields wider CIs... should be interpreted cautiously"）。
- R1 建议将 Cohen's d 提到正文——同意这一具体建议。但将此列为 Must-Fix 过重；qualitative conclusion 不受 K=11 影响。**Should-Fix 更合适。**

---

### Should-Fix

**[AGREE] R1-W1**: Pure-strategy 设计高估 death asymmetry
- 同意。42.9% internal death rate 是纯 internal 策略的 worst-case 上界。实际 mixed-strategy router 会在部分 steps 使用 deterministic，降低 death rate。论文的 oracle 分析（Table 2, §3.5）部分回应了这一点（oracle 96.3% 选择 deterministic，death rate 14.3%），但没有量化 transferability gap。
- 不过论文的 framing 是 "diagnostic framework"——目的是分析 routing signal 的组成，而非预测 mixed-strategy 性能。这在一定程度上缓解了 R1 的担忧，但论文确实应更明确区分 "diagnostic finding" 和 "deployment implication"。

**[AGREE] R1-W2**: Figure 2 caption 缺 "mathematical consequence" caveat
- 同意。Figure 2 caption（experiments.tex line 10-11）仅写 "r = 0.97, p < 10^{-6}, n = 11 task types"，没有提及 r→1 是 death dominance 在 constant P 下的数学必然（正文 §3.1 有讨论，但 caption 是独立阅读单元）。快速浏览的审稿人会误解为独立的经验发现。
- 注：R1 原文写 "Figure 1"，但根据 experiments.tex，scatter plot 是 Figure 2 (fig:decomposition)。Figure 1 是 pipeline overview。

**[AGREE] R1-W3**: 72B DAF 对比缺关键细节
- 同意。§3.3（experiments.tex line 61）报告 72B DAF=90.9%，但未说明 deterministic strategy 用的是 72B 还是 7B。从 Table 1 上下文看，deterministic baseline (16.3%) 来自 7B。如果 72B DAF 是用 72B internal vs 7B deterministic 计算的，这是不对称的对比。72B 模型运行 deterministic strategy 时的 death rate 可能与 7B 不同（虽然 deterministic 策略理论上不依赖 LLM 推理质量，但 action parsing 等可能有差异）。作者应明确说明并最好补充 72B deterministic death rate。

**[REBUT] R1-W4**: 27.7% mislabeling fraction 对 78.9% 的影响
- 反驳。这里有 level-of-analysis 混淆。27.7% mislabeling（Limitations, main.tex line 39）描述的是 step-level labels 与 episode-level labels 的不一致——即 "episode 最终标注为 det-preferred，但其中某些 steps 的 per-step oracle 会选择 internal"。这是 episode-level labeling 的固有 tradeoff，论文已在 §2.2 充分论证了为什么 step-level labeling 在 sparse-reward 环境下退化（97.4% ties）。
- 78.9% 是 **episode-level** metric，不受 step-level mislabeling 影响。Episode-level labels 的可靠性由 Labeling Quality Audit（Appendix B）保证："Zero labels depend on tie-breaking"（line 94）。
- R1 的担忧方向应该是 "episode-level labels 是否是好的 routing target"，而非 "27.7% 影响 78.9% 的诊断准确性"。前者是 methodology limitation（已在 Limitations 讨论），后者不成立。

**[AGREE] R1-W5**: 缺少 permadeath 环境复制
- 强烈同意，与我的 N2 完全一致。这是论文最大的完整性缺口。

**[AGREE] R1-W6**: Data scaling 用 paraphrase augmentation 而非 real data
- 同意，但加一个 nuance。论文自己在 Appendix F（line 369）承认 "paraphrase augmentation inflates the majority class without generating novel routing patterns; real-data scaling remains an open question"。问题是正文 §3.7 和 Discussion §5 中的 "structural failure" 结论措辞过于绝对。
- 真正的 bottleneck 是 3.7% internal-preferred base rate（论文计算需要 ~1350 paired episodes 才能获得 50 个 internal-preferred 样本，Appendix F line 393），这是实验设计的 intrinsic 限制，而非 structural impossibility。将 "structural failure" 改为 "failure under current data regime" 更准确。

---

### R1 的 Questions 补充评论

**Q1**（72B deterministic 模型）：已在 W3 中讨论，同意需要澄清。

**Q2**（find-non-living-thing n=40 是否 data-dependent）：Table 3 脚注（main.tex line 124）承认 "data was collected in two batches, with the second batch adding 20 episodes to increase statistical power for this zero-death outlier"。这是 data-dependent decision，但方向是增加而非减少样本量，不构成 p-hacking。Minor 问题。

**Q3**（Reflexion 是否改变 Δ_nd）：论文未报告 Reflexion 的 Δ_nd，这是一个重要遗漏。如果 Reflexion 在降低 death rate 的同时也改变了 non-death performance gap，那么 DAF 的变化可能反映不同的 underlying mechanism。同意这值得补充。

**Q4**（DAF 95% CI 是 episode-level 还是 cluster-level）：正文 §3.1 报告的 [81.6%, 98.8%] 是 episode-level bootstrap（method.tex line 67: "episode-level bootstrap resampling (B=10,000)"）；cluster-level CI [73%, 100%] 在 Appendix D (Table 6) 和 Limitations 中报告。这两个 CI 在正文中的区分不够清晰。

**Q5**（Inverted-U 仅基于 15 episodes）：Discussion §5 (line 13) 提到 "below ~0.5B, agents fail to reach dangerous states (13.3% death rate in a 15-episode pilot)"。15 episodes 确实太少，只能作为 anecdotal evidence。论文将其标为 hypothesis 而非 finding 是合适的，但如果要在 Practitioner Decision Framework（Appendix L）中引用，需要更多数据。

---
